mantis_shrimp.title: THIS SHRIMP PUNCHES SO FAST IT BOILS WATER
mantis_shrimp.script: This is a mantis shrimp, and its punch is one of the most violent attacks in the ocean. Its front appendages snap forward with extreme acceleration, striking hard-shelled prey like crabs and snails. The blow is so fast that it creates vapor bubbles in the water. When those bubbles collapse, they release a second shock wave called cavitation. Its eyes are also extraordinary, with a complex visual system that can detect polarized light. This small crustacean combines a shell-smashing weapon with one of the strangest sensory systems in the ocean.
mantis_shrimp.caption: Mantis shrimp are built like underwater weapons. #AnimalFacts #MantisShrimp #OceanFacts #WildVox

owl.title: THIS BIRD HUNTS IN NEAR SILENCE
owl.script: An owl can turn its head up to 270 degrees without cutting off blood flow. Its eyes are large and fixed in their sockets, so the neck has to do the tracking. Many owls have asymmetrical ear openings that help them compare tiny timing differences in sound and pinpoint prey in darkness. Their facial disc funnels sound toward the ears. Soft fringes on the feathers also break up turbulence and reduce noise. By the time a mouse hears an owl coming, the attack may already be over.
owl.caption: Owls are built to hunt in near silence. #AnimalFacts #Owl #Wildlife #WildVox

shark.title: IT CAN FEEL ELECTRICITY
shark.script: A shark is a living sensory machine. Its skeleton is made of cartilage instead of bone, making the body lighter and flexible. Around the snout are special organs called the ampullae of Lorenzini. They can detect extremely weak electrical fields produced by the muscles and nerves of other animals, helping a shark locate prey even in poor visibility. Sharks also replace teeth throughout their lives, with new rows moving forward as older teeth are lost.
shark.caption: Sharks can detect electrical signals from living animals. #AnimalFacts #Shark #OceanFacts #WildVox

frog.title: THIS ANIMAL DRINKS THROUGH ITS SKIN
frog.script: Frogs do not always drink water the way mammals do. Many absorb it directly through a specialized patch of skin on the belly and thighs. That skin also plays a major role in breathing, which is one reason frogs need to stay moist. Their tongue is attached near the front of the mouth, allowing it to flip outward rapidly and grab prey. In many frogs, the eyes can retract downward while swallowing and help push food toward the throat.
frog.caption: Frogs can absorb water directly through their skin. #AnimalFacts #Frog #Wildlife #WildVox
